name: Silk'n Infinity / Flash&Go

lead: Silk'n makes home light-based hair-removal devices, including the Infinity and Flash&Go lines, used for gradual hair reduction and smoother, less hairy skin. They use low-energy pulsed light designed for self-treatment.

Home pulsed light is absorbed by hair melanin and heats the follicle, so hair thins across sessions. A 2009 study of an early Silk'n home device tested 34 people and 92 sites with blinded hair counts and reported hair reduction; the Infinity and Flash&Go models themselves have no trial in the sources reviewed.

paras: Users flash the device over shaved skin in repeated sessions over weeks, then maintain occasionally. Home IPL suits darker hair on lighter skin.
A 2010 review of home IPL devices noted they are designed to damage follicles, with eye safety a key design concern. Home-use IPL is generally considered less suited to very dark skin or light hair.

angle.text: Users apply Silk'n Infinity and Flash&Go devices at home for gradual hair reduction. Home pulsed light hits the follicles, so hair thins across sessions and skin looks smoother. A small 2009 study of an early Silk'n device reported hair reduction; the current models are less studied.

lead: Silk'n is a brand of home light-based hair-removal devices, including the Infinity and Flash&Go models. An early device from the brand, made by HomeSkinovations of Israel, was described in a 2009 study as a small, light-weight, low-energy, low-cost IPL system for home use. [1]

The 2009 study tested the device on 34 people and 92 sites, with self-treatment supervised in clinic and hair counts done by a blinded observer. [1] The sources reviewed contain no trial specific to the Infinity or Flash&Go models.

paras: A 2009 study of the Silk'n home pulsed light device on 34 people and 92 test sites used pre- and post-treatment hair counts analysed by a blinded observer. [1] A 2014 IRB-approved study of 17 subjects examined the separate Silk'n Blue device for inflammatory acne, with eight treatments over four weeks, and reported a statistically significant decrease in acne lesions. [2] A 2023 study compared a home-use laser with a diode laser for hair reduction. [3]

A 2010 review of home-use IPL devices stated that such systems are designed to cause biological damage and that eye safety is a central design requirement. [4] Encyclopedic sources list hyperpigmentation among IPL complications. [5]
